about.title: Porterville Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Porterville residents rely on a handful of local clinics and Tulare County medical facilities for everything from emergency care to ongoing treatment, and most visits go fine. But when a provider misses a diagnosis, makes a surgical error, or mishandles medication, the consequences can be serious and lasting. California law treats these cases differently than a typical injury claim — there are shorter deadlines, a required 90-day notice before filing suit, and rules that make expert medical testimony essential to prove your case. A bad outcome by itself isn't proof of malpractice; the law requires showing the provider fell below an accepted standard of care. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself, but we can connect Porterville residents with an independent attorney who understands MICRA's requirements and can review what happened at no upfront cost.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in Porterville?
items.answer: California generally allows one year from when you discover the injury, but no more than three years from the date it occurred. Before filing a lawsuit, state law also requires giving the healthcare provider 90 days' notice. These deadlines are strict, so it helps to talk with an attorney as soon as you suspect something went wrong.

items.question: Is a poor medical result automatically malpractice?
items.answer: No. California law recognizes that medicine involves risk, so a disappointing outcome alone doesn't prove negligence. To have a valid claim, you generally need a qualified medical expert to show the provider's care fell below the accepted standard — this is why professional review matters.

items.question: Are there limits on what I can recover in a malpractice case?
items.answer: California caps non-economic damages, like pain and suffering, in medical malpractice cases, though that cap rises each year under current law. Economic losses, such as medical bills and lost income, aren't subject to the same cap. An independent attorney can walk through how this applies to a Porterville case.
